message.content:
**Famous American Composers (by era)**  

| Composer | Lifespan | Notable Works / Contributions |
|----------|----------|--------------------------------|
| **William Billings** | 1726–1770 | “The Battle of Trenton” – one of the first American choral works; pioneer of early American hymnody. |
| **John Philip Sousa** | 1854–1932 | “The Stars and Stripes Forever,” “Washington Post March” – “The March King” of the U.S., shaped the American march tradition. |
| **George Gershwin** | 1898–1937 | “Rhapsody in Blue,” “An American in Paris,” “Porgy & Bess” – bridged classical and jazz idioms. |
| **Aaron Copland** | 1900–1990 | “Appalachian Spring,” “Rodeo,” “Fanfare for the Common Man” – “Father of the American sound.” |
| **Leonard Bernstein** | 1918–1990 | “West Side Story,” “Candide,” “On the Town” – celebrated conductor, composer, and educator. |
| **Philip Glass** | 1937– | Minimalist style; “Einstein on the Beach,” “Glassworks” – influential in contemporary classical music. |
| **John Williams** | 1942– | Film scores for “Star Wars,” “Indiana Jones,” “Jurassic Park” – one of the most recognizable film composers worldwide. |
| **Steve Reich** | 1936– | “Music for 18 Musicians,” “Different Trains” – pioneer of minimalism and tape music. |
| **John Adams** | 1947– | “Short Ride in a Fast Machine,” “Nixon in China” – modernist composer blending minimalism with orchestral color. |
| **Martha Argerich** | 1941– | Though primarily a pianist, her interpretations of American composers like Copland and Gershwin have been influential. |
| **Kurt Weill** | 1900–1950 | “The Threepenny Opera,” “Mahagonny” – German-born but made significant contributions to American musical theater. |
| **Charles Ives** | 1874–1954 | “The Unanswered Question,” “Concord Sonata” – early modernist experimenting with polytonality. |
| **Samuel Barber** | 1910–1981 | “Adagio for Strings,” “Knoxville: Summer of 1915” – known for lyrical, emotionally resonant works. |
| **Elliott Carter** | 1908–2012 | “Variations on a Theme of Frank Bridge,” “Symphony No. 1” – advanced rhythmic complexity and serial techniques. |

### How “famous” is measured
- **Historical impact** (e.g., Billings, Sousa)
- **Cultural reach** (e.g., Gershwin, Copland)
- **Contemporary influence** (e.g., Glass, Reich, Adams)
- **Popular recognition** (e.g., John Williams)

These composers represent a broad spectrum of American musical history—from early colonial hymnody to modern minimalism and blockbuster film scores. Their works continue to shape both concert halls and popular culture worldwide.
